title: We Cannot See You
subtitle: Amelia Earhart & Fred Noonan · Pacific Ocean, 1937
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Desaturated documentary still, the open central Pacific Ocean in July 1937, vast grey-blue swells and hazy tropical light, 1930s period detail, melancholy and uncanny, cinematic wide composition, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no signage, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: July second, nineteen thirty-seven. Amelia Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, left New Guinea for tiny Howland Island.
beats.img: A twin-engine silver 1930s airliner-style monoplane seen small and distant from behind, climbing away over a dark tropical coastline into a hazy morning sky above the open Pacific, no markings visible, no people.

beats.vo: A Coast Guard ship waited off Howland, listening. Earhart radioed: we must be on you, but cannot see you.
beats.img: The dim radio room of a 1930s ship at dawn, a brass-and-bakelite radio receiver with glowing dials, a headset resting on a wooden desk beside a blank logbook and a pencil, grey light through a porthole, no people.

beats.vo: About an hour later, one of her last messages. A line of position. No reference point.
beats.img: A tiny flat sandy island seen from far out at sea under a hazy morning sky, a lone ship anchored offshore trailing a thin column of dark smoke, vast empty ocean, no people.

beats.vo: The search found no trace of the plane, or of either of them.
beats.img: A 1930s naval vessel small on an immense empty grey Pacific under low cloud, wide aerial view, endless swells, searching, no people visible.

beats.vo: Nearly ninety years on, the plane has never been found.
beats.img: A remote uninhabited tropical atoll at dusk, a shallow lagoon and a reef edge with surf, dense dark scrub, a pale empty beach, the open Pacific beyond, quiet and unresolved, no people.

facts.claim: On July 2, 1937, Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan took off from Lae, New Guinea, bound for Howland Island, a small US island in the central Pacific
US Coast Guard cutter Itasca was stationed off Howland Island to provide radio/navigation support
At 7:42 a.m. Earhart radioed 'We must be on you, but cannot see you' (Itasca radio log)
At 8:43 a.m. (about an hour later) the last message heard by Itasca gave a line of position 157-337, 'running north and south', with no reference point
Navy and Coast Guard search ended July 19, 1937, finding no physical evidence of Earhart, Noonan or the Electra
Leading theories: ran out of fuel and crashed at sea (US government conclusion, most historians); landed on Gardner Island/Nikumaroro to the south(east) and died as castaways. Neither proven

Plane never found as of Oct 2026: Deep Sea Vision's Jan 2024 sonar target was confirmed a rock formation (Nov 2024); the ALI/Purdue Taraia Object survey on Nikumaroro (Oct 2026) had NOT identified the object as of Oct 16, 2026
